newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia public lack policymakers' optimism.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia public lack policymakers' optimism.

text.p: The Australian economy is well positioned to strengthen through 1997 and into 1998, policymakers say, and generally analysts tend to agree.
The trouble is consumers and business do not seem to share that optimism, according to two surveys released on Wednesday.

Despite the fourth rate cut since last July being delivered on May 23 and the federal budget on May 13 that lacked any major spending cuts, consumer sentiment is at its lowest level in almost two years and business confidence has also fallen.
High unemployment, an inability of firms to pass on price increases and a patchy economy have dented confidence.

The Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index for June fell 2.4 percent and Westpac's general manager of economics, Bill Evans, expressed surprise, given the fact the survey was taken two weeks after the latest rate cut.
This was the index's third successive fall, and left it at 100 points, its lowest level since September 1994.
"Evidence from this survey indicates that for the time being unemployment may have taken over from interest rates as the most important influence on consumer sentiment," Evans said.
Unemployment has been unable to break below 8.5 percent over the past two and a half years, and the government has forecast it to fall only to 8.0 percent by the June quarter next year.

Consumers were more pessimistic in June about economic prospects over the next year, with people reporting a rise in unfavourable news about unemployment and less favourable news, despite the rate cut and benign budget, Evans said.

Business shares consumers' pessimism. The National Australia Bank May Business Survey found that confidence continued to fall despite the recent rate cut, with repondents reporting disparate business conditions across sectors.
There was little sign of a generalised economic pick-up, and confidence was further dented by falls in profitability and employment indicators.

"Services continue to perfrom relatively well, but manufacturing, wolesaling and, to a lesser extent, retailing continue to report poor conditions," the NAB survey found, adding that mining also reported poor conditions in May for the first time since late 1995.
One of the few positives in the business survey was a significant fall in labour costs in May, which should help ease the pain of a continued squeeze on operating margins.
Policy makers, however, have been more optimistic.

"Overall, 1997 looks like being a year of stronger growth than 1996," Reserve bank of Australia governor Ian Macfarlane said last month when announcing the latest rate cut which saw official rates drop to 5.50 percent.
"Longer-term prospects for growth are also good, and are helped by the ongoing fiscal consolidation confirmed in the recent budget," Macfarlane said.

Treasurer Peter Costello is also optimistic on the economy gaining pace as 1997 progresses. "This is a good outcome and a pointer to very favourable prospects in the forthcoming year, Costello said after last week's release of first quarter gross domestic product data showing a 0.9 percent rise.
Financial markets expect the Australian economy to continue on a low inflation-strong growth trajectory after a soft finish to 1996.
"We agree with the pronouncements of the local authorities that Australia is now set to record stronger growth over the course of 1997," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said.
"The impetus will come from stocks, housing, consumption and exports with business investment holding up."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
